passage: Playground note, Friday (Class 3 teacher). Mehak (8) would not walk past the old banyan by the back gate today. She held my hand and asked if a lady in white really lives in it. On Monday she laughed when Sonali first told the story. By Wednesday, four more girls had 'heard it too,' and the lady now 'cries at lunchtime' and 'took a boy's shoe.' Today Mehak whispered, 'Everyone says so, Miss, so it must be real.' I didn't argue. We walked to the tree together, looked at the roots and a squirrel's nest, and counted who had actually seen anything: nobody. On Monday I will ask the class where each version of the story started.

qa.q: What did Mehak do when Sonali first told the story on Monday?
qa.a: Mehak laughed.

qa.q: Why had Mehak come to believe the story by Friday?
qa.a: Hearing it from more and more girls, each adding new details, made it feel true; Mehak said everyone says so, so it must be real.

qa.q: What did the teacher choose to do instead of arguing, and why might it work?
qa.a: The teacher walked Mehak to the tree and counted who had actually seen anything, letting Mehak notice that many retellings came from zero sightings.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel on Monday when the class traces where the story started?
qa.a: Sonali might feel surprised, and a little sheepish, to see how a small story grew so big once everyone kept retelling it.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child believing a haunted-tree story more after hearing it retold by many classmates.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today is Thursday and now I am scared of the tamarind tree. On Monday Swati said a ghost goat lives in it. I said goats can't be ghosts. On Tuesday Raju said he heard it bleat at night. On Wednesday, three kids said the watchman saw red eyes. Today at lunch EVERYONE was talking about it, even the Class 6 boys, and they said it chews the swings. The swings DO have marks. So maybe it's true?? So many people can't be making it up. I walked the long way round to the tap so I didn't have to pass it.
Tomorrow I'll ask Swati who told her first.
— Neelam

qa.q: What did Raju say about the tree on Tuesday?
qa.a: Raju said he heard it bleat at night.

qa.q: Why did Neelam start to believe in the ghost goat by Thursday?
qa.a: Neelam felt more scared each day as more and more people repeated the story, until it seemed true simply because so many were saying it.

qa.q: Is asking Swati who told the story first a good next step for Neelam? Why?
qa.a: Yes, because tracing it back could show the story began with one person's tale, not with anyone who actually saw something.

qa.q: What might Swati feel if Neelam asks where the story came from?
qa.a: Swati might realise the tale grew far bigger through retelling, and could feel surprised or a bit guilty that Neelam got scared.

grounding: A child's diary shows belief in a ghost story growing each day as more classmates repeat it.

passage: Gargi had fetched water past the old peepal by the village pond a hundred times. Then, on the walk home from school, Neelam said her cousin had seen a lantern moving in its branches at night. The next day the milkman's son said the lantern floated. By Saturday, women at the hand pump were saying a spirit swung from the lowest branch and tugged at dupattas. Gargi's Dadi clicked her tongue, but even she walked a little faster past it. That evening Amma asked Gargi to bring water. Gargi stood at the door, pot on her hip, staring at the dark tree. "Everyone says it," she whispered. "Everyone." She waited until her brother could come along.

qa.q: Who said the lantern floated?
qa.a: The milkman's son.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling while standing at the door with the pot?
qa.a: Gargi was afraid of a tree that had never scared her before, because so many people now repeated the spirit story. 😟

qa.q: When Gargi hesitated at the door, what could Amma have done?
qa.a: Amma could ask who had actually seen anything and walk to the pond with Gargi, showing that the story grew by retelling, not by new sightings.

qa.q: Why might Dadi walking faster matter to Gargi?
qa.a: When even a grown-up seemed uneasy, Gargi took it as more proof, so Dadi's small reaction made the story feel even more real.

grounding: A village girl grows afraid of a familiar tree as a spirit story spreads and grows through repetition.

passage: On Monday, Ingrid told Astrid that the big oak by the school fence in Uppsala had a face in its bark. Astrid, nine, went to look. It was just a knot. On Tuesday, two boys said the face moved its mouth when it rained. On Wednesday, the whole of Class 3 knew that a girl had lost her glove near the roots and never found it, because the oak took it. By Thursday, people ran past it with their hoods up. Astrid did too. On Friday, Ingrid's brother said a teacher had seen it breathe. Astrid had stopped looking at the oak at all. She walked the long way round the football pitch, just in case.

qa.q: What did Astrid find when she first went to look at the bark?
qa.a: It was just a knot.

qa.q: Why did Astrid start walking the long way round, even though she had seen only a knot?
qa.a: Hearing the story from more and more people made it feel truer and scarier, so she avoided the oak just in case.

qa.q: At which point could Astrid have tested the story, and how?
qa.a: Early in the week she could have asked who actually saw the mouth move, or looked at the knot again with a teacher in daylight.

qa.q: How might a teacher feel on hearing children say a teacher had seen the oak breathe?
qa.a: The teacher might be amused but also concerned that the children are frightened, and want to talk about how stories grow.

grounding: A child believes the haunted-tree story more each time more classmates repeat it.

passage: Lights-out at the residential school outside Nashik was at nine, and that was when the stories started. The first night, Madhav whispered from the top bunk that the old gulmohar behind Dormitory B dropped flowers only on boys who were going to fail. Darshan, eleven, snorted. The second night, someone in the next row added that a watchman had heard crying in its branches. The third night it was four voices, and the crying had a name. By Saturday, boys carried their buckets the long way to the bathroom block. Darshan told himself it was silly. But when a red flower landed on his shoulder at morning PT, his heart thudded, and he brushed it off before anyone could see.

qa.q: When did the stories start at the school?
qa.a: They started at lights-out, at nine.

qa.q: What does Darshan brushing the flower off before anyone could see suggest?
qa.a: Though he called the story silly, hearing it night after night had made it feel real enough to scare him, and he didn't want others to notice.

qa.q: How could a house parent help after hearing the story grow each night?
qa.a: They could talk calmly with the boys about how a tale grows with each telling, and walk them past the tree in daylight.

qa.q: How might Madhav feel if he learned the story he started now frightened Darshan?
qa.a: Madhav might feel surprised and a little guilty that one whisper grew into something so big.

grounding: A child comes to half-believe a haunted-tree story as it is retold each night by more voices.
